video.title: Charts that tell the truth: Bar, line, pie and scatter
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Ms Salma - the students' geography teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our class drew our town's rainfall as a pie chart. Twelve slices, one for each month. Nobody could see when the rains came. The data was right, but the chart was wrong.
Today: which chart fits which question, and how charts can mislead.
A bar chart compares groups. Which fruit does our class like best? One bar for each fruit, and the tallest bar wins. Mango wins easily here, with eleven pupils.
A line chart shows change over time. Rainfall month by month makes a line that rises in the rainy season and falls again. Now everyone can see when the rains come.
A pie chart shows how one whole is shared out, like the school budget: books, repairs, sports and food. Use it only with a few slices that add up to the whole.
A scatter chart puts two measurements of each pupil on one picture, like hours of reading and spelling marks. Each dot is one pupil. If the dots rise together, the two go together.
Now a trick to watch for. Our pass rate went from seventy to seventy four percent. If the axis starts at sixty eight, the new bar looks three times taller. Bars must start at zero.
Quick check! You measured a bean plant every day for two weeks. Which chart shows how it grew?
A line chart. The days go along the bottom, the height goes up, and the line shows the growth over time. You can even see the days when it grew fastest.

scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: pick the right chart
scenes.narration: In the app, open Pick the right chart. Match five questions to their charts, then drag where the axis starts and watch a small change look huge.
Your turn. A poster shows two bars, and the axis starts at ninety. What should you check first?
Where the axis starts. Remember: bars compare groups, lines show time, pies show parts of a whole, and scatter shows two measurements. And bars start at zero.
Try it yourself: draw a bar chart of your family's favourite foods, with a title, labels and a scale from zero. Show it to someone and ask what they can tell from it.

checkpoints.prompt: You measured a bean plant every day for two weeks. Which chart shows how it grew?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: change over time belongs on a line chart.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the plant changes day by day, so a line chart shows its growth best.

checkpoints.prompt: A poster's bar chart has an axis starting at 90. What should you check first?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: an axis that does not start at zero makes small differences look big.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: look at where the axis starts. Starting at 90 exaggerates the difference.
